title: Hoarding and squalor
audience: Coordinators, support workers and trained cleaners who may be asked to work in a home affected by hoarding or environmental neglect, as part of an authorised support plan. Not a qualification or authority to clear a property, dispose of a resident's belongings, enter by force, or provide welfare or clinical support.
referencesAtStart: Official sources for this lesson: CFA, Hoarding and fire safety (last updated 22 September 2026); WA Health, Help with hoarding (last reviewed 16 July 2026); FRV, Hoarding and environmental neglect; DFFH, Hoarding and environmental neglect.

subLessons.title: Fire loads, heating and electrical ignition
Safe handling and staged work zones
Privacy, tenant rights and multidisciplinary handoff

learningOutcomes: Define the scope of work from the resident-approved objective, and distinguish a safety improvement from a full-property clearance.
Obtain specific, documented consent for each area, action and possession, and refuse to treat access to a property as permission to dispose of its contents.
Communicate respectfully with residents and support people, avoid humiliating images, and keep information confidential.
Recognise combustible loads, heating and electrical ignition sources, and blocked alarms or escape paths, and escalate fire-risk decisions to competent services.
Map safe egress and emergency access before any material is staged, and recognise when an obstruction must be moved under authority.
Recognise piles and shelving that may collapse, and withdraw from an unstable zone until a competent assessment is made.
Recognise pests, droppings, mouldy goods and unknown liquids as hazards outside ordinary cleaning, and route them for specialist assessment without probing enclosed spaces.
Recognise sharps, unlabelled containers and unknown materials, stop handling, isolate the area and escalate to trained personnel.
Plan small, staged work zones with lifting limits, clean and dirty separation, and a daily inventory review.
Separate waste into authorised, retained, recyclable, unknown and regulated streams, and refuse any transfer into general waste whose stream is unknown.
Apply privacy, tenancy and information-sharing limits, and refuse unauthorised collection or publication of personal information.
Record partial outcomes honestly, arrange follow-up, and avoid claiming that a one-time clear-out is a lasting remediation.

instruction.heading: Module authority and restricted work
instruction.body: This module is training content. It does not grant authority to enter a home by force, to clear, sort or dispose of a resident's belongings without valid consent, to handle or dispose of hazardous waste, to deal with unstable stacks or structural hazards, or to provide welfare, clinical or safeguarding assessments. Completing this lesson does not give a licence, certificate or approval. Work is done only under an authorised support plan and a written agreement with the resident, within the limits set by the employer and the local law. Tenancy, safeguarding and information-sharing rights are jurisdiction-specific, and fire-risk, structural, pest and hazardous-waste decisions belong to the competent authorities and specialists named in the plan. Where authority or consent is unclear, stop and refer.

instruction.heading: 1. Scope, goals and client-defined success
instruction.body: Work to the resident-approved objective. A safety improvement is different from a full-property clearance, and the worker should not drift from one to the other. Distinguish the contractual instructions from the resident's rights and from the limits of the worker's own skills. The site-specific risk assessment and the authorised support plan take precedence over any generic example. Ask the resident to describe what must remain untouched, and record the areas permitted for work and the decisions that need fresh permission. Record what was seen directly, what was reported by others, and what is still unverified. Changes to the agreed scope need supervisor clearance. Permission is not inferred from a deadline or from the presence of keys. In a scenario where a property manager demands the removal of all contents while the resident has authorised only the clearing of an access route, the worker compares the work order with the resident's choices and documents a limited, approved safety goal. Without a consent-based scope the worker does not proceed, and the disagreement is recorded and referred.

instruction.heading: 2. Consent, belongings and decision authority
instruction.body: Consent must be specific to the area, the action and the possession. Access to a property is not blanket permission to dispose of its contents. Use an item-decision log with the categories retain, relocate, undecided and authorised disposal, and let the resident revisit decisions. A relative who asks the crew to discard sealed boxes while the resident is away does not hold that decision. Pause the handling, seek a valid documented authority and consent decision, and leave the contested items where they are. In training, create an item-by-item keep, relocate, review or discard process, and pause every contested removal.

instruction.heading: 3. Respectful communication and coordinated support
instruction.body: Do not frame clutter or environmental neglect as a personal failure. Avoid humiliating photographs and coercive tactics. Agree communication roles, breaks, privacy rules and an escalation contact with the resident, and invite only the supporters the resident has authorised. A worker who shares a before-photograph to a group chat without permission has breached privacy and must stop sharing, follow the privacy and incident procedure, and preserve confidentiality. In training, rewrite the conversation and set a consent-based escalation to a support coordinator.

instruction.heading: 4. Fire loads, heating and electrical ignition
instruction.body: Combustible storage near a heat source or an electrical ignition point, together with obstructed alarms or escape routes, increases the consequence of a fire. Identify urgent hazards from a safe vantage point, and refer fire-risk decisions to the competent local fire service when the situation calls for it. Do not disturb unstable stacks. Suspend work in the affected areas and escalate the fire or access hazard. A situation in which paper is stacked around a heater and a door cannot fully open is a stop-work situation. In training, map the no-touch ignition risks and propose authorised, low-disruption risk reduction steps, without proposing electrical or heating work.

instruction.heading: 5. Safe egress and emergency access
instruction.body: An improvement plan must keep safe access and exit available for residents, workers and emergency responders. Map the agreed entrance, exits, trip hazards and emergency meeting points before any materials are staged. If a cart or stack blocks the only practical exit during work, stop, move the obstruction safely where that is authorised, and recheck the evacuation paths before work continues. In training, draw an evacuation-path plan and decide whether safe work can proceed without disturbing the stacks.

instruction.heading: 6. Structural instability and unstable piles
instruction.body: Piles, overloaded shelving and damaged floors can hide a collapse risk. Use a no-disturbance inspection boundary, and identify the signs that need a structural or specialist opinion. A cabinet that leans into a tower of boxes, combined with water damage on the floor, is a sign of instability. Withdraw from the unstable zone and obtain a competent assessment before any load is changed. In training, recognise the instability and issue a stop-work notice together with a qualified inspection referral.

instruction.heading: 7. Pests, contamination and hygiene triage
instruction.body: Droppings, insects, mouldy goods and unknown liquids may need controls that are outside ordinary cleaning competence. Screen the area visually and do not probe enclosed spaces. Document the indicators and route them for specialist assessment. Restrict access to the affected area and avoid any action that creates aerosols, such as dry sweeping or vacuuming, until approved contamination guidance has been obtained. A sealed storage room with a strong odour and visible droppings is an example. In training, separate observation from diagnosis, isolate the area and request a specialist risk evaluation.

instruction.heading: 8. Sharps, chemicals and unknown materials
instruction.body: Unidentified needles, unlabelled containers and potentially hazardous waste must not enter ordinary rubbish handling. A loose needle among clothes beneath unknown bottles is a stop-work situation. Cease handling in the area, isolate it and escalate to suitably trained personnel. Prepare a hazard log without touching the suspect items, and explain the isolation and referral procedure. Do not open, sort or move unknown containers. In training, demonstrate the stop-work boundary and the specialist waste and health escalation using inert props only.

instruction.heading: 9. Safe handling and staged work zones
instruction.body: Controlled work in small areas reduces re-accumulation, manual-handling strain and the loss of items the resident values. Agree small work zones, a work and rest pattern, safe lifting limits and a daily inventory review with the resident. A crew that rushes several rooms at once and mixes keepsakes with waste has breached the agreed plan. Stop the process, restore the separation of clean and dirty items, and audit any unapproved change with the resident. In training, plan short sessions, lifting controls, clean and dirty separation and safe traffic routes.

instruction.heading: 10. Waste, reuse and property records
instruction.body: Waste categories and disposal authority differ by material and by jurisdiction, and traceability matters. Separate the authorised ordinary waste from retained, recyclable, unknown and regulated streams, and record the approved destination of each. A skip contractor who declines a leaking, unidentified container has made a correct decision. Do not transfer that container into general waste. Record it and seek a compliant specialist pathway. Record the owner of each item and the permission to remove it, keep reusable property separate, and confirm that each waste destination is lawful. In training, complete the records for a fictional job and confirm the destinations.

instruction.heading: 11. Privacy, tenant rights and multidisciplinary handoff
instruction.body: Tenancy rights, safeguarding referrals and information-sharing permissions are jurisdiction-specific. Apply the approved communication plan and give access to records only on the minimum-necessary basis. Refer welfare concerns clearly to the people responsible for them. Before collecting or disclosing any private information, check the legal authority, the purpose and the consent. An agency that asks for photographs of every room and of personal documents is asking for more than the work requires. Refuse unauthorised publicity and document the lawful permissions, the confidentiality and the service referrals that apply. In training, prepare the handoff record for a fictional case.

instruction.heading: 12. Verification, follow-up and recurrence prevention
instruction.body: A one-time clear-out does not, on its own, establish sustained safety, a change in habits or a clinical outcome. Where a doorway is clear but a blocked exit elsewhere remains unresolved, the job is only partly complete, and the outstanding safety issue must be referred. Document the partial outcome honestly and do not claim full remediation. In training, record the outcomes that have been achieved without claiming a cure, and set out the future support and maintenance follow-up.

instruction.heading: Stop-work and referral rules for this module
instruction.body: Stop and refer whenever any of these is true: consent is not specific, documented and current; the resident has objected or withdrawn consent; a party seeks entry by force, nonconsensual disposal or removal of personal documents; a fire-load, ignition, egress or obstruction hazard is present; a stack or structure is unstable; pests, unknown liquids or mouldy goods are present; sharps, chemicals or unknown containers are found; waste would go to general disposal without characterisation; private information is requested without authority; or the work would go beyond the approved plan. Stopping is a valid professional outcome. Record the disagreement, protect the resident's choices and refer the authority dispute before any property is moved.

procedure: Stop. Do not move or dispose of any item until the consent for that item is documented and current.
Record the resident's objective, the areas and actions permitted, and the items that need fresh permission.
If a fire, egress, structural, pest, sharps or unknown-material hazard is present, suspend work in the affected area and do not disturb the stack or material.
Refer the hazard to the competent service, the specialist or the emergency service named in the plan, and record the referral.
Protect the resident's dignity and privacy. Take no images beyond the authorised record, and do not share any information.
Separate waste into streams and send only the authorised ordinary waste to ordinary disposal. Refer all other streams to a compliant pathway.
Record the decisions, the permissions, the disagreements and the referral recipients in the job file.
Issue a partial-outcome handover that records what was achieved, what remains unresolved and the follow-up that has been arranged.

workedExamples.situation: A property manager demands removal of all contents while the resident has authorised only clearing an access route.
workedExamples.reasoning: The approved boundary is the access route the resident has authorised. The manager's demand is not a resident decision. Document the limited, approved safety goal, record the disagreement, and refer the authority dispute before any item is moved.

workedExamples.situation: A relative asks the crew to discard sealed boxes while the resident is away.
workedExamples.reasoning: Pause. The relative does not hold the decision, and access to the home is not consent to dispose of belongings. Leave the sealed boxes in place and seek a valid, documented consent decision.

workedExamples.situation: Paper is stacked around a heater and a door cannot open fully.
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop work in the affected area and escalate the fire and access hazard to the competent service. Do not disturb the stacks. Map the no-touch ignition risks and agree low-disruption reduction steps with the resident.

workedExamples.situation: A cabinet leans into a tower of boxes, and the floor shows water damage.
workedExamples.reasoning: Withdraw from the zone. Signs of instability require a competent assessment before any load is changed. Issue a stop-work notice and a qualified inspection referral.

workedExamples.situation: A loose needle appears among clothes beneath unknown bottles.
workedExamples.reasoning: Cease handling in the area and isolate it. Do not touch or sort the materials. Escalate to suitably trained personnel and record the hazard log.

workedExamples.situation: A skip contractor declines a leaking, unidentified container.
workedExamples.reasoning: The contractor's refusal is correct. Do not transfer the container into general waste. Record it and seek a compliant specialist pathway.

workedExamples.situation: An agency asks for pictures of every room and of personal documents.
workedExamples.reasoning: Refuse unauthorised publicity. Check the legal authority, the purpose and the consent before any private information is collected or disclosed, and document the decision.

equipmentAndPpe: PPE selected from the hazard assessment in the support plan, with the worker's training verified by the employer. Respiratory protection only where the assessment requires it, under the employer's program.
Item-decision log and labelled retain, relocate, review and authorised-disposal categories.
Lifting aids and safe lifting limits set in the agreed plan.
Barrier tape, signage and a clean and dirty separation plan agreed with the resident.
Hazard log, referral records and the waste-stream register.
Training-only props, mock records and role-play. No real sharps, unknown containers, pests, stacks or waste are handled in this lesson.

commonErrors.error: Treating access to the home as permission to clear everything.
commonErrors.prevention: Limit work to the consent that is documented, specific and current. Refer any broader demand.

commonErrors.error: Discarding a relative's or manager's choices about the resident's belongings.
commonErrors.prevention: Pause the contested removal and obtain a valid, documented decision from the resident.

commonErrors.error: Framing the clutter as the resident's failing, or taking humiliating photographs.
commonErrors.prevention: Use person-centred language and take no images beyond the authorised record.

commonErrors.error: Sharing a photograph of a resident's home to a group chat.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop sharing, follow the privacy and incident procedure, and keep the information confidential.

commonErrors.error: Moving a stack to make a path, without a competent assessment.
commonErrors.prevention: Withdraw from the unstable zone and refer for a structural assessment before any load is changed.

commonErrors.error: Dry sweeping or vacuuming droppings or mouldy goods.
commonErrors.prevention: Restrict access, avoid aerosol-producing actions and obtain approved contamination guidance.

commonErrors.error: Handling an unknown container or needle to see what it is.
commonErrors.prevention: Cease handling, isolate the area and escalate to trained personnel.

commonErrors.error: Putting unknown or leaking containers into general waste.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the item and seek a compliant specialist pathway.

commonErrors.error: Telling the resident or agency that the home is now fully remediated after a one-time clear-out.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the partial outcome honestly, refer the outstanding risks and arrange follow-up.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: This module does not grant authority to clear or dispose of belongings, enter by force, handle hazardous waste or unknown materials, deal with unstable structures or provide welfare or clinical assessment. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.
Waste handling, hazardous-material handling and some structural and fire-risk work are restricted to competent and, where required, licensed people.

Sources recorded for this lesson include Victorian, Western Australian and New South Wales agencies, a London fire brigade and a Victorian council. The London source is not Australian law. The sources are person-centred guidance, not legal determinations.
Consent is specific to the area, the action and the possession, and it can be withdrawn. Access to a property is not consent to dispose of its contents.
No forced entry, nonconsensual disposal, unstable-stack disturbance, unassessed contamination or hazardous-waste work is part of this module. The approved plan and local procedures apply.
No product, method, dilution or quantity is given for any cleaning, pest, chemical or waste task.
Information about a resident's health, drug use or personal circumstances is sensitive. Disclosure follows privacy law and the authority that holds the record.

qualityStandard: The learner identifies the consent that exists for each area and action, and refuses work outside it.
The learner pauses a contested removal and records the disagreement and the decision authority.
The learner recognises the fire, egress, structural, pest, sharps and unknown-material hazards in a described scene and stops work with a referral.
The learner routes waste into streams and refuses general disposal of material of unknown stream.
The learner refuses unauthorised collection or publication of personal information.
The learner writes a partial-outcome handover that claims no full remediation and arranges follow-up.
documentationEvidence: Resident-approved objective and the scope record, with permitted areas and decisions needing fresh permission.
Item-decision log with the retain, relocate, undecided and authorised-disposal categories, and the resident's dated decisions.
Consent record, communication plan and the escalation contact.
Hazard log for fire, egress, structural, pest, sharps and unknown-material indicators, with referral records.
Evacuation-path plan and the access map agreed with the resident.
Staged work-zone plan with lifting limits and a daily inventory review.
Waste-stream register with the approved destination for each stream, and reuse records for retained property.
Privacy and information-sharing record, with the lawful basis for each disclosure.
Partial-outcome handover with achieved outcomes, unresolved risks and arranged follow-up.
summary: Consent comes first. It is specific, documented, current and can be withdrawn.
Access to a home is not permission to dispose of its contents.
Use person-centred language. Do not frame clutter as personal failure.
Stop at fire loads, blocked exits, unstable stacks, pests, sharps and unknown materials. Refer them.
Keep exits open and map evacuation paths before staging anything.
Work in small, agreed zones with a daily inventory review.
Route waste by stream. Never send unknown or leaking material to general waste.
Protect privacy. Do not share images or information without authority.
A one-time clear-out is a partial outcome. Record it honestly and arrange follow-up.

knowledgeChecks.question: A property manager demands removal of all contents, but the resident has authorised only clearing an access route. What is the approved boundary?
options: The access route the resident has authorised, with the disagreement recorded and the authority dispute referred.
All contents, because the manager is the client and the manager has the final say on the whole job
Whatever the crew can move in one day, since the rest can be left for another visit later on the job

knowledgeChecks.question: A relative asks the crew to discard sealed boxes while the resident is away. What must the worker do?
options: Discard them, because the relative is family and knows what the resident would want
Pause, leave the boxes in place and seek a valid, documented consent decision.
Discard them and photograph them first, so there is a record of the items

knowledgeChecks.question: Paper is stacked around a heater and a door cannot open fully. What should happen?
options: Clear the paper quickly so the door opens, since the stacks are only paper and cause no danger to anyone
Move the heater to the other room, so that the paper is no longer near the heat source for long
Stop work in the affected area, do not disturb the stacks and escalate the fire and access hazard.

knowledgeChecks.question: A cabinet leans into a tower of boxes, and the floor shows water damage. How is the zone treated?
options: Withdraw from the zone and obtain a competent assessment before any load is changed.
Brace the cabinet with boxes and continue the clean, since the boxes will hold it steady for now
Remove the top boxes and continue carefully, since lighter loads are safer to move on the floor

knowledgeChecks.question: A loose needle appears among clothes beneath unknown bottles. What is the correct response?
options: Pick up the needle with gloves and bag it, since the gloves protect the hands from the sharp end
Cease handling in the area, isolate it and escalate to suitably trained personnel.
Sort the clothes to find any other needles before the crew moves on to the next room today

knowledgeChecks.question: A skip contractor declines a leaking, unidentified container. What is the right course?
options: Put the container into general waste, because the skip is full and the crew needs to leave the site today
Pour out the contents to make the container safe to carry, so it can be placed in the van
Accept the refusal as correct, record the container and seek a compliant specialist pathway.

knowledgeChecks.question: An agency asks for pictures of every room and of personal documents. What is the response?
options: Refuse unauthorised collection and publication, and check the legal authority, purpose and consent first.
Provide them, because the agency is involved in the case and needs the records to close the file
Provide pictures of the rooms only, since the agency has a right to see the rooms but not the documents

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker shares a before-photograph of a resident's home to a group chat. What must happen?
options: Nothing, because the group is supportive and the photo is only shared with friends
Stop sharing, follow the privacy and incident procedure, and preserve confidentiality.
Delete the photograph from the group and continue with the rest of the job as planned

knowledgeChecks.question: Droppings and mouldy goods are found in a sealed storage room. What is the correct approach?
options: Dry sweep the droppings and bag the goods, since the bags will keep the mess contained
Open the room windows and clean as usual, since the air will clear the room quickly
Restrict access, avoid aerosol-producing actions and obtain approved contamination guidance.

knowledgeChecks.question: A crew rushes several rooms at once and mixes keepsakes with waste. What should happen?
options: Stop the process, restore the separation and audit any unapproved change with the resident.
Continue, because the rooms are nearly finished and the crew is almost done for the day
Put all the keepsakes in the waste to speed up the work and finish the rooms today

knowledgeChecks.question: A one-time clear-out is complete. What can be reported to the resident and the support team?
options: The home is fully remediated and will stay that way, since the clear-out was thorough and complete
The partial outcome achieved, the unresolved risks and the arranged follow-up, without claiming a cure.
The home is safe to live in with no further support needed from the team or the family

knowledgeChecks.question: A blocked exit elsewhere in the home remains unresolved, though the doorway is now clear. What is correct?
options: Report the job as complete, because the doorway is clear.
Leave the blocked exit for the resident to deal with.
Document the partial outcome and refer the outstanding exit hazard.

officialReferences.title: Hoarding and fire safety
officialReferences.covers: Read via summary tool (page heading 'Hoarding and fire safety'; the URL read is the CFA fire-risks page). Hoarding makes fires more likely and more dangerous; blocked hallways and doors can stop escape and rescue; hoarded items can reduce sprinkler effectiveness in apartments. One-off clean-ups do not address the reasons behind hoarding, and long-term support from health and human services is advised. Publisher: Country Fire Authority (Victoria).

officialReferences.title: Help with hoarding
officialReferences.covers: Read via summary tool: get the person's permission before touching or removing their things; cleaning begins only after the person agrees to take steps to clean their living space; a written agreement can list which items will be removed. The page also lists support services (GP referral, NDIS, My Aged Care, helplines). Publisher: WA Department of Health (healthywa).

officialReferences.title: Hoarding (Fire Rescue Victoria)
officialReferences.covers: Read 2026-11-03 (page title 'Hoarding'; the source title 'Hoarding and environmental neglect' did not match a page on the search). FRV reports attending a fire or emergency involving hoarding or environmental neglect every 4 to 6 days; hoarding increases fire risk; accumulated possessions create an abnormally high fuel load; FRV recommends risk reduction as a priority rather than large-scale removal. The page does not say that one-off clean-ups are inadequate, so that point is not supported by this entry.

officialReferences.title: Hoarding and environmental neglect
officialReferences.covers: Victorian DFFH provider page titled Hoarding and environmental neglect: defines hoarding, distinguishes it from collecting, and points service providers to the Make Safe guidance. Publisher: Department of Families, Fairness and Housing (Victoria).
